name: Berlin
tagline: History in the open, nights that run late
summary: Berlin is spread out, so group sights by district: the government quarter and Museum Island, then the Wall sites, then Kreuzberg and Neukölln for food. Many memorials are free.
seasonNote: Winters are cold and grey, but Christmas markets fill late November and December.
arrival: Airport express and regional trains reach the centre from BER in 30 to 40 minutes.
gettingAround: The U-Bahn, S-Bahn and trams cover everything; validate paper tickets before boarding.
cashTip: Cash is still preferred at many small restaurants, kiosks and bars; carry euros.
foodTip: Eat a döner kebab, currywurst and a slice of cake at afternoon Kaffee und Kuchen.
buyTip: Design and vintage from Kreuzberg and Mitte shops; flea market finds at Mauerpark on Sundays.

connections.note: Direct EuroCity trains along the Elbe valley.
Direct trains several times a day.
Air time only; trains take around 7 hours.

items.name: Brandenburg Gate
items.summary: The neoclassical gate that stood in no man's land and became the symbol of reunification.
items.expect: A quick stop that is always busy.
items.tip: Come at sunrise or after dark, and walk on to the Holocaust Memorial.
items.why: No other monument sums up Berlin's divided and reunited history as well.
flow: Approach along Unter den Linden.
Walk through to the Tiergarten side.

items.name: Reichstag Dome
items.summary: The German parliament, topped by a glass dome with a spiral ramp and free audio guide.
items.expect: Free, but advance registration with passport details is required.
items.tip: Register online weeks ahead and bring the same ID.
items.why: You look down on the debating chamber and out over the whole government quarter.
flow: Pass security with your booking.
Walk the spiral ramp with the audio guide.

items.name: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe
items.wiki: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe
items.summary: A field of 2,711 concrete blocks, with an underground information centre.
items.expect: A sombre place; the centre has security checks and closes on Mondays.
items.tip: Walk into the middle of the field, then visit the centre below.
items.why: It is the country's central Holocaust memorial and an unforgettable piece of design.
flow: Walk through the blocks.
Go down to the information centre.

items.name: Museum Island and the Neues Museum
items.summary: Five museums on a river island; the Neues Museum holds the bust of Nefertiti.
items.expect: The Pergamon Museum is closed for long-term renovation; check which halls are open.
items.tip: Pick one or two museums; a day ticket covers all that are open.
items.why: The ensemble is a World Heritage site with world-class antiquities.
flow: See Nefertiti in the Neues Museum.
Add the Alte Nationalgalerie, then the cathedral outside.

items.name: East Side Gallery
items.summary: The longest surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall, painted with murals in 1990.
items.expect: A roadside walk of 1.3 km with selfie crowds at the famous panels.
items.tip: Start at Ostbahnhof and finish at the Oberbaum Bridge.
items.why: It is the Wall as open-air gallery, including the 'Fraternal Kiss'.
flow: Walk the river side of the wall.
Cross the Oberbaum Bridge into Kreuzberg.

items.name: Berlin Wall Memorial
items.summary: A preserved section of the border strip with a watchtower, viewing platform and documentation centre.
items.expect: Outdoor panels over several blocks; indoor centres close on Mondays.
items.tip: Climb the viewing platform to see the death strip from above.
items.why: It is the clearest place to understand how the Wall actually worked.
flow: Start at the visitor centre near Nordbahnhof.
Follow the strip to the viewing platform.

items.name: Mustafa's Gemüse Kebap
items.summary: A famous kiosk for chicken döner with roasted vegetables, feta and lemon.
items.expect: Queues of 30 minutes or more.
items.tip: Go mid-afternoon on a weekday, or try a neighbourhood döner shop instead.
items.why: The döner is Berlin's own street food and this is its best-known version.
flow: Join the queue.
Order a chicken döner or the vegetarian version.

items.name: Curry 36
items.summary: A stand-up snack bar that is the reference point for Berlin currywurst.
items.expect: Standing tables on the pavement.
items.tip: Order it 'ohne Darm' (without skin) with fries and mayonnaise.
items.why: Currywurst was invented in Berlin, and this stand has served it since 1980.
flow: Order at the window.
Eat at a standing table.

items.name: Markthalle Neun
items.summary: A restored 1891 market hall with craft food stalls and a Thursday street food night.
items.expect: Limited stalls early in the week; very busy on Thursday evenings.
items.tip: Come for Street Food Thursday or Saturday's full market.
items.why: It is the centre of Berlin's independent food scene.
flow: Walk the hall once.
Share plates from several stalls.

items.name: Prater Garten
items.summary: Berlin's oldest beer garden, under chestnut trees since 1837.
items.expect: Outdoor season only, roughly April to September; self-service.
items.tip: Bring cash and go on a warm evening.
items.why: The simplest way to spend a summer evening the local way.
flow: Fetch beer and food from the kiosks.
Share a long bench under the trees.

name: Prague
summary: See Charles Bridge and the castle at the edges of the day and spend the busy middle hours in quieter quarters. The centre is compact but cobbled and hilly.
seasonNote: Summer and December market season are packed; January to March is cold and quiet.
arrival: A trolleybus and the metro take about 45 minutes from the airport; use official taxi stands or apps.
gettingAround: Walk the centre; trams are frequent and tram 22 is a sightseeing ride in itself.
cashTip: Pay by card or use bank ATMs; avoid street exchange offices and decline card conversion.
foodTip: Try svíčková, roast pork knuckle, fried cheese and a properly poured tank pilsner.
buyTip: Bohemian glass, garnet from certified shops and wooden toys; skip the generic souvenir chains.
baseArea: Old Town edge, Malá Strana or Vinohrady

connections.note: Direct Railjet trains every two hours.
Direct trains by day; a flight takes about an hour.

items.name: Charles Bridge
items.summary: A 14th-century stone bridge lined with 30 statues, joining the Old Town to the castle side.
items.expect: Shoulder-to-shoulder from mid-morning to evening.
items.tip: Cross at sunrise; climb the Old Town bridge tower for the view.
items.why: It is the city's defining walk, with the castle rising ahead.
flow: Enter under the Old Town bridge tower.
Cross to Malá Strana and look back.

items.name: Prague Castle and St. Vitus Cathedral
items.summary: A hilltop complex of palaces and churches around a soaring Gothic cathedral.
items.expect: Security checks at the gates and queues for the cathedral.
items.tip: Enter at opening from the tram 22 stop and see the cathedral first.
items.why: It is among the largest castle complexes in the world, with the country's finest stained glass.
flow: Visit St. Vitus, the Old Royal Palace and Golden Lane.
Walk down the castle steps to Malá Strana.

items.name: Old Town Square and Astronomical Clock
items.summary: The medieval main square, with the Týn church and a clock that has run since 1410.
items.expect: A crowd gathers on the hour for a 45-second show.
items.tip: Climb the Old Town Hall tower rather than waiting for the chime.
items.why: It is one of Europe's best-preserved medieval squares.
flow: See the clock strike the hour.
Take the lift up the tower.

items.name: Jewish Quarter (Josefov)
items.summary: Historic synagogues and a centuries-old cemetery of layered gravestones.
items.expect: One combined ticket; closed Saturdays and Jewish holidays.
items.tip: Start at the Pinkas Synagogue, whose walls list the names of victims.
items.why: It is the best-preserved Jewish quarter in central Europe.
flow: Pinkas Synagogue and the Old Jewish Cemetery.
Then the Spanish Synagogue.

items.name: Petřín Hill
items.summary: A wooded hill with orchards, a small lookout tower and wide views over the city.
items.expect: A steep walk; check whether the funicular is running.
items.tip: Walk up through the orchards and down past Strahov Monastery.
items.why: It is the greenest viewpoint and far calmer than the castle terraces.
flow: Climb or ride up.
Go up the lookout tower, then walk to Strahov.

items.name: Vyšehrad
items.summary: A quiet riverside fortress with ramparts, a neo-Gothic church and a cemetery of national figures.
items.expect: Few tourists; a short metro ride from the centre.
items.tip: Walk the ramparts at sunset and visit Dvořák's grave.
items.why: It has castle-level views without the crowds.
flow: Enter by the Tábor Gate.
Circle the ramparts and visit the cemetery.

items.name: Lokál Dlouhááá
items.summary: A long beer hall serving fresh tank Pilsner and careful versions of Czech classics.
items.expect: Noisy and full at night.
items.tip: Reserve, or come for a late lunch.
items.why: It is the reliable place for well-kept beer and honest Czech cooking in the centre.
flow: Order a 'hladinka' pour.
Share fried cheese, then svíčková or schnitzel.

items.name: Café Louvre
items.summary: A grand café from 1902, once used by Kafka and Einstein.
items.expect: Busy at breakfast; steady service.
items.tip: Good for breakfast or cake and Czech hot chocolate.
items.why: It is the most authentic of Prague's surviving First Republic cafés.
flow: Go upstairs to the main room.
Order breakfast or dessert.

items.name: U Fleků
items.summary: A brewery pub brewing its own dark lager on site since 1499.
items.expect: Tour groups, accordion music and trays of shots you can decline.
items.tip: Say no to the offered liqueur unless you want to pay for it.
items.why: It is the oldest brewpub in Prague, and the dark lager is made only here.
flow: Sit in the courtyard or a hall.
Order the house dark lager and goulash.

items.name: Naplavka riverside and farmers' market
items.summary: A riverside quay with a Saturday farmers' market and summer bars on boats and in vaults.
items.expect: The market runs Saturday mornings; evening bars are seasonal.
items.tip: Go on Saturday morning for pastries, sausages and coffee by the water.
items.why: It is where locals spend warm evenings and weekend mornings.
flow: Browse the stalls.
Eat on the quay wall.

name: Vienna
tagline: Imperial palaces, music and coffee houses
summary: Mix one palace, one museum and one coffee house per day. The Ring boulevard holds most sights, and Schönbrunn needs a half day of its own.
seasonNote: December Christmas markets are a peak; January and February are cold and quiet.
arrival: The S7 train and the City Airport Train reach the centre in 16 to 25 minutes.
gettingAround: The U-Bahn and trams are excellent; a 24 to 72 hour pass is good value.
cashTip: Cards are widely accepted, but some coffee houses, sausage stands and markets prefer cash.
foodTip: Have a Wiener schnitzel, a Käsekrainer from a sausage stand and cake with a melange.
buyTip: Chocolates and Sachertorte to take home, Augarten porcelain and Manner wafers.
baseArea: Inside or just outside the Ring; Neubau for a local feel

connections.note: Direct Railjet trains every two hours.

items.name: Schönbrunn Palace
items.summary: The Habsburgs' summer palace: gilded state rooms and formal gardens climbing to the Gloriette.
items.expect: Timed palace tickets that sell out by midday in season.
items.tip: Book online; the gardens are free and the Gloriette has the view.
items.why: It is Austria's most visited sight and the full picture of imperial life.
flow: Take the palace tour.
Walk up through the gardens to the Gloriette.

items.name: St. Stephen's Cathedral
items.summary: The Gothic cathedral at the city's centre, with a patterned tile roof and climbable towers.
items.expect: Free to enter the back; the nave, towers and catacombs are ticketed.
items.tip: Climb the 343 steps of the south tower for the roof view.
items.why: It has been the heart of Vienna for 700 years.
flow: Walk the nave.
Climb the south tower or take the north tower lift.

items.name: Hofburg and Sisi Museum
items.summary: The Habsburgs' city palace, with the imperial apartments and the Sisi Museum.
items.expect: A big complex with separate tickets for separate parts.
items.tip: Choose between the apartments, the treasury and the Spanish Riding School.
items.why: Six centuries of empire were run from these courtyards.
flow: Walk in from Michaelerplatz.
Visit the Sisi Museum and imperial apartments.

items.name: Kunsthistorisches Museum
items.summary: The imperial art collection, with the world's largest group of Bruegel paintings.
items.expect: Closed on some Mondays; a lavish building that is a sight itself.
items.tip: Have coffee under the dome between galleries.
items.why: Bruegel, Vermeer, Raphael and Velázquez hang in rooms built for them.
flow: Go up to the picture gallery.
Finish in the Kunstkammer.

items.name: Belvedere
items.summary: Two baroque palaces and a garden; the Upper Belvedere holds Klimt's The Kiss.
items.expect: Timed entry and a crowd around The Kiss.
items.tip: Book a morning slot and walk the gardens down to the Lower Belvedere.
items.why: It has the largest Klimt collection anywhere.
flow: See the Klimt rooms upstairs.
Walk down through the terraced garden.

items.name: Vienna State Opera
items.summary: One of the world's great opera houses, with nightly performances and daytime tours.
items.expect: Seats sell out; cheap standing tickets go on sale on the day.
items.tip: Try for standing-room tickets, or take the 40-minute guided tour.
items.why: Hearing music here is the essential Vienna evening.
flow: Take an afternoon tour.
Or queue for standing room before a performance.

items.name: Figlmüller
items.summary: The best-known schnitzel house, serving plate-overhanging pork schnitzel since 1905.
items.expect: Bookings fill weeks ahead; walk-ins queue.
items.tip: Reserve online, and order potato salad on the side.
items.why: It is the classic place for the city's signature dish.
flow: Arrive for your booking.
Share a schnitzel with potato-lamb's lettuce salad.

items.name: Café Central
items.summary: A vaulted 1876 coffee house once frequented by Freud and Trotsky.
items.expect: A queue outside for much of the day.
items.tip: Go at opening or book a table online.
items.why: It is the grandest of Vienna's coffee houses, with live piano in the afternoon.
flow: Wait to be seated.
Order a melange and a slice from the cake counter.

items.name: Naschmarkt
items.summary: A long open-air market of produce, spices, cheese and small restaurants.
items.expect: Closed on Sunday; samples are pressed on you along the main aisle.
items.tip: Eat at the far end where prices drop; a flea market runs on Saturdays.
items.why: It is Vienna's biggest market and an easy lunch between sights.
flow: Walk from the Secession end.
Stop for a plate at a stall restaurant.

items.name: Café Sacher
items.summary: The hotel café that serves the original Sachertorte, created in 1832.
items.expect: A queue and a formal room; the cake is dense and not very sweet.
items.tip: Always have it with unsweetened whipped cream.
items.why: It is the home of the world's most famous chocolate cake.
flow: Queue or book.
Order Sachertorte with cream and coffee.

name: Budapest
tagline: Thermal baths and a river of lights
summary: Spend one day on hilly Buda and one on flat Pest, with a long thermal soak in between. The Danube view after dark is the highlight, and it is free.
seasonNote: Summer is hot and festival-heavy; December brings Christmas markets.
arrival: The 100E express bus runs from the airport to the centre in about 40 minutes.
gettingAround: Metro, trams and buses share one ticket; tram 2 follows the river for the views.
cashTip: Pay in forints by card and decline conversion to your home currency; avoid Euronet ATMs.
foodTip: Try goulash soup, chicken paprikash, lángos and a chimney cake.
buyTip: Paprika, Tokaji wine and Herend or Zsolnay porcelain.
baseArea: District V, VI or VII in Pest

connections.note: Air time only; buses take about 7 hours.

items.name: Hungarian Parliament Building
items.summary: A vast neo-Gothic parliament on the Danube, with a gilded staircase and the Holy Crown.
items.expect: Guided tours only, and they sell out in summer.
items.tip: Book online ahead; see it lit up at night from the Buda bank.
items.why: It is the city's signature building, inside and out.
flow: Take the 45-minute tour.
Walk south to the Shoes on the Danube memorial.
items.best: Morning tour; evening from across the river

items.name: Fisherman's Bastion and Matthias Church
items.summary: White turreted terraces beside a tile-roofed church, looking over the Danube and Parliament.
items.expect: Crowded from mid-morning; the upper turrets are ticketed in the daytime.
items.tip: Come at sunrise, when it is empty and free.
items.why: It is the best view of Pest and the Parliament.
flow: Walk the terraces.
Go inside Matthias Church.

items.name: Buda Castle
items.summary: The former royal palace on Castle Hill, now home to the National Gallery and history museum.
items.expect: A long walk across the hill; the funicular has queues.
items.tip: Walk up from the Chain Bridge or take bus 16.
items.why: The hill's courtyards and terraces are free and wide open.
flow: Go up from Clark Ádám Square.
Cross the courtyards towards Matthias Church.

items.name: Széchenyi Thermal Bath
items.summary: A yellow neo-baroque bath palace with large outdoor thermal pools open all year.
items.expect: Busy at weekends; bring flip-flops and a towel or rent them.
items.tip: Go on a weekday morning and book a cabin rather than a locker.
items.why: Soaking outdoors in steaming water is the essential Budapest experience.
flow: Change and head to the outdoor pools.
Try the indoor pools and saunas.

items.name: St. Stephen's Basilica
items.summary: The city's largest church, with a dome terrace that looks over all of Pest.
items.expect: Ticketed entry, with separate tickets for the dome.
items.tip: Take the lift to the dome terrace near sunset.
items.why: The 360-degree terrace is the best view on the Pest side.
flow: See the interior.
Go up to the panoramic terrace.

items.name: Jewish Quarter and Szimpla Kert
items.summary: The old Jewish quarter, with Europe's largest synagogue and the 'ruin bars' in derelict courtyards.
items.expect: Party crowds at night; calmer by day and at the Sunday farmers' market.
items.tip: See the Dohány Street Synagogue by day and Szimpla Kert in the early evening.
items.why: The ruin bars started here and are unique to Budapest.
flow: Visit the Dohány Street Synagogue.
Walk Kazinczy Street to Szimpla Kert.

items.name: Central Market Hall
items.summary: A huge 1897 iron market hall with produce and paprika downstairs and food stalls upstairs.
items.expect: Closed on Sunday; the upstairs food counters are crowded and pricey.
items.tip: Buy paprika and salami downstairs; eat one lángos upstairs.
items.why: It is the best single stop for Hungarian ingredients.
flow: Walk the ground-floor aisles.
Go up for lángos.
order: Lángos with sour cream and cheese

items.name: New York Café
items.summary: A gilded, frescoed 1894 café often called the most beautiful in the world.
items.expect: Queues and very high prices for average food.
items.tip: Book a table and order only coffee and cake.
items.why: The interior is extraordinary.
flow: Wait to be seated.
Order coffee and a dessert.

items.name: Gettó Gulyás
items.summary: A small restaurant specialising in Hungarian stews and goulash.
items.expect: Often fully booked in the evening.
items.tip: Reserve ahead or try for lunch.
items.why: It serves well-made versions of the national dishes at fair prices.
flow: Start with goulash soup.
Share a paprikash with nokedli dumplings.

items.name: Gerbeaud
items.summary: A chandeliered pastry house on the main square, open since 1858.
items.expect: Tourist prices and a slow pace.
items.tip: Try the layered Gerbeaud slice or Esterházy torte.
items.why: It is the city's most historic confectioner.
flow: Take a table in the salon.
Order a classic cake with coffee.

name: Copenhagen
summary: A compact, flat capital best seen by bike or on foot: the harbour and palaces by day, Tivoli after dark. It is expensive, so mix bakeries and food halls with one special dinner.
seasonNote: Summer days are very long; winter is dark, but Tivoli's Christmas season is a draw.
arrival: The metro and trains reach the centre from the airport in 15 minutes.
gettingAround: Walk, cycle or use the metro and harbour buses, which share one ticket.
cashTip: Almost entirely cashless; a card or phone is all you need.
foodTip: Eat smørrebrød at lunch, a cinnamon or cardamom bun, and a hot dog from a pølsevogn.
buyTip: Danish design homeware, ceramics and licorice.

connections.note: Air time only; trains take about 7 hours.
Air time only; add airport transfers.

items.name: Nyhavn
items.summary: A 17th-century canal lined with brightly painted houses and old wooden ships.
items.expect: Expensive terraces on the sunny side.
items.tip: Photograph it from the bridge, then start a canal tour here.
items.why: It is the postcard image of Copenhagen.
flow: Walk the sunny side.
Take a one-hour canal tour from the quay.

items.name: Tivoli Gardens
items.summary: An amusement park and garden from 1843, with rides, lanterns and concerts.
items.expect: Entry and rides are charged separately; closed between seasons.
items.tip: Go in the evening when the lights come on.
items.why: It is one of the oldest amusement parks in the world and a real local favourite.
flow: Enter before dusk.
Ride the 1914 wooden roller coaster, then watch the lights.

items.name: Rosenborg Castle
items.summary: A small Renaissance castle holding the Danish crown jewels, set in the King's Garden.
items.expect: Timed tickets in summer; narrow rooms.
items.tip: Book a slot and picnic in the garden afterwards.
items.why: The treasury in the cellar holds the crowns and regalia.
flow: Tour the royal rooms.
Go down to the treasury.

items.name: Christiansborg Palace
items.summary: The seat of parliament, with royal reception rooms and a free tower view.
items.expect: Security at the tower; several separately ticketed areas.
items.tip: The tower is free and the tallest in the city.
items.why: It combines royal halls, medieval ruins and a top view in one stop.
flow: Go up the tower.
Visit the royal reception rooms.

items.name: The Little Mermaid and Kastellet
items.summary: The small bronze mermaid on a harbour rock, beside a star-shaped fortress.
items.expect: Smaller than people expect, with a constant crowd.
items.tip: Walk or cycle there along the harbour and loop back through Kastellet's ramparts.
items.why: It is the city's emblem, and the walk is the best part.
flow: Follow the waterfront from Amalienborg.
Return over Kastellet's ramparts.

items.name: Freetown Christiania
items.summary: A self-governing community of murals, workshops and self-built houses in old barracks.
items.expect: An alternative atmosphere; respect residents' rules, including on photography.
items.tip: Walk the lakeside path beyond the centre to see the handmade houses.
items.why: It is a one-of-a-kind social experiment from 1971.
flow: Enter by the main gate.
Follow the path around the lake.

items.name: Torvehallerne
items.summary: Two glass market halls with more than 60 stalls, from smørrebrød to porridge and coffee.
items.expect: Packed at weekend lunchtimes.
items.tip: Have open sandwiches at Hallernes Smørrebrød.
items.why: It is the easiest place to try Danish food at moderate prices.
flow: Walk both halls.
Eat at a counter or outside.

items.name: Schønnemann
items.summary: A lunch restaurant from 1877 that sets the standard for traditional smørrebrød.
items.expect: Lunch only; booked out days ahead.
items.tip: Reserve, and let the staff pair the snaps.
items.why: It is the classic place for open sandwiches done properly.
flow: Start with herring.
Move on to a warm dish such as fried plaice.

items.name: Reffen
items.summary: A large open-air street food market in an old shipyard on the harbour.
items.expect: Seasonal, roughly April to September, and weather-dependent.
items.tip: Take the harbour bus there for sunset.
items.why: It is the best casual dinner with a view in summer.
flow: Arrive by harbour bus.
Pick a stall and sit by the water.

items.name: Sankt Peders Bageri
items.summary: The city's oldest bakery, known for giant cinnamon rolls on Wednesdays.
items.expect: A queue on Wednesday, when the 'onsdagssnegl' is sold.
items.tip: Any day is fine; go early for the widest choice.
items.why: It is a classic stop for real Danish pastry.
flow: Queue at the counter.
Take a cinnamon roll to go.
